Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/AP US Senate Murkowski won’t vote for Trump’s nomination of Blanche as attorney general Alaska Republican is concerned that proposed fund to compensate January 6 rioters will proceed even though Blanche confirmed it was dead US politics live – latest updates Guardian staff and agency Fri 7 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 08.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Lisa Murkowski, Alaska’s moderate Republican senator, announced early on Friday that she will not vote for Donald Trump’s nomination of Todd Blanche as US attorney general, leaving his elevation from “acting” to official confirmation in the post even narrower. Murkowski issued a statement expressing her concerns that the Trump administration could proceed with its proposed fund to compensate rioters who invaded the US Capitol on January 6 in a failed attempt to overturn Joe Biden’s defeat of Trump in the 2020 presidential election. She took her stance even though Blanche confirmed in writing the controversial fund was dead. Experts say Trump could easily reverse it. Murkowski said the Senate only currently has leverage over the fund because Blanche’s nomination to head the Department of Justice is pending necessary confirmation by the upper congressional chamber. Blanche had persuaded the Senate judiciary committee in a 12-10 vote in his favor earlier this week only because he promised Republican holdouts that he would not pursue the payout fund. Blanche issued a formal order late on Sunday terminating Trump’s $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” slush fund designed to compensate political allies who had been “targeted” by the justice department, including prosecutions of January 6 insurrectionists. That move followed weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators who were blocking his nomination to become attorney general – Thom Tillis and John Cornyn, who were eventually swayed by Blanche. Murkowski posted on X on Friday, praising Blanche but then saying “ultimately” she would oppose his nomination, a position she took on Tuesday and is now sticking with. “The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration. I hope Mr Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case,” she wrote, as part of a much longer post on the topic. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, but Mitch McConnell of Kentucky is not currently attending sessions because of his health, giving the GOP little room to lose senators and still confirm the president’s pick. The Associated Press contributed reporting. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Russia’s defence minister, Andrey Belousov, pins the Gold Star Hero of Russia medal on Maj Gen Anton, who two weeks later has been killed in Ukraine. Photograph: Russian Defence Ministry/Reuters View image in fullscreen Russia’s defence minister, Andrey Belousov, pins the Gold Star Hero of Russia medal on Maj Gen Anton, who two weeks later has been killed in Ukraine. Photograph: Russian Defence Ministry/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Drone kills Russian commander just decorated after fake victory claim Maj Gen Anton Grunis was praised by Vladimir Putin for purported capture of Kostiantynivka; UK names intel officer who died in Ukraine road crash. What we know on day 1,667 Warren Murray and agencies Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.21 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukrainian drone forces have killed a Russian general who had just been made a Hero of Russia after false claims that Moscow’s forces had captured the Donetsk city of Kostiantynivka. Maj Gen Anton Grunis died in eastern Ukraine on Saturday. “General Grunis was ​eliminated on September 12,” said Ukrainian drone commander Robert Brovdi, adding that the general was the seventh Russian military commander killed by his drone forces. Another Russian commander, Apti Alaudinov, posted confirmation that Grunis had died. The battle for Kostiantynivka is gruelling for Ukraine but war analysts say it remains contested. Grunis reported personally to Vladimir ​Putin earlier this year that his troops helped capture Kostiantynivka and was praised by the Russian president for “doing the work”. The territorial claim ⁠remains heavily disputed – the US-based Institute for the Study of War said Russian forces ​had infiltrated but not fully ​seized the city, and ​Russia’s claim was part of a wider information campaign to “portray the Ukrainian frontlines ​as collapsing”. Grunis received the Gold Star Hero of Russia award at a ceremony in late August. Russian ⁠airstrikes damaged buildings in Kyiv ​and injured three in the Black ⁠ Sea port city of Odesa in the ⁠early hours of Thursday, officials ​said. In Kyiv, debris fell ‌on ‌warehouses and near ‌a petrol station, among other locations, said the mayor, Vitali ‌Klitschko. Three people, including a ⁠child, were injured as Russia ​hit a ​19-storey apartment ​building in Odesa, authorities said. Russian drones struck a passenger bus, killing five people, as well as attacking a train in southern Ukraine on Wednesday, Ukrainian officials said. “There is no military logic to this, ⁠just another act of brutality,” said the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The bus was hit near the frontline city of Nikopol. Seven more people were wounded, said the Dnipropetrovsk region’s governor. Russian drones attacked a passenger train three times in Ukraine’s southern Mykolaiv region, the acting regional governor said. Passengers and crew were evacuated and no one was hurt. Zelenskyy said that ‌in addition, a locomotive was struck in Kovel near the border with Poland. Russian shelling on Wednesday killed one person in the southern Kherson region, and in the port of Odesa one death was reported. Russian attacks injured more than a dozen people in Sumy in the north and Kropyvnytskyi in central Ukraine. The Russia-installed head of areas of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region held by Moscow ⁠said a Ukrainian drone strike killed one person. Officials in Russia’s border Belgorod region said six ​people were injured in Ukrainian attacks. The Russian Gerbera-2 drone found in the Baltic Sea off Poland was armed with explosives, officials said on Wednesday. Polish defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Monday that the military had located the drone near the village of Rusinowo in north-western Poland and recovered it from the sea. The drone was thought to have been lost by Russia during test manoeuvres over the Baltic. Polish military prosecutors are investigating whether legal proceedings can be launched, presumably against Russia, for “causing an incident that endangers the life or health of many people and property of great value”. The Russian government has extended a ban on diesel ⁠exports until the end of October. ​The ban had been due to end this month. Russia introduced restrictions on exports of gasoline, jet fuel and diesel because of domestic ⁠fuel shortages driven by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries. Reuters reported that fuel market data indicates three of Russia’s six largest diesel-producing refineries ​were forced to significantly cut output or halt production altogether in September because of damage caused by drone attacks. Russia’s Rosneft-owned oil refineries in the Volga river cities of ⁠Syzran and Saratov have stopped ⁠processing after ​Ukrainian drone attacks this month, Reuters reported on Wednesday citing three industry sources. Britain’s defence ministry has named a 40-year-old intelligence officer who died in a road crash away from the frontlines in Ukraine on Saturday. Maj Paul Wilks was commissioned from Sandhurst in 2012 and joined the Intelligence Corps, where he remained throughout his career. His commanding officer described Wilks as a “man of great intellect”, who often spoke of his love for his wife and two sons. Maj Paul Wilks, who died in a road crash away from the frontlines in Ukraine on 12 September. Photograph: Ministry of Defence/PA The chief of defence intelligence described Wilks as “one of the most talented intelligence officers of his generation”. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said Wilks “served this country with pride and dedication”. A small number of British personnel serve in Ukraine providing security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces. Britain’s MoD previously announced paratrooper George Hooley, 28, was killed in Ukraine in December as he watched Ukrainian forces testing a new defensive capability. A Russian strike destroyed a warehouse in Kyiv that stored props for Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s former TV studio, the company said on Wednesday, adding that its staff were unharmed. Zelenskyy co-founded the Kvartal 95 production company in 2003 while working as a comedian. “We lost a large number of sets, costumes, and items that for 20 years had been part of our concerts, TV shows, movies, and series,” Kvartal 95 said. Zelenskyy spent much of his early career working in television, including in Russia. In 2013, he co-presented Russian state TV’s New Year’s Eve show. Kvartal 95 ceased work in Russia following Moscow’s annexation of Crimea in 2014. https://www.politico.eu/article/swedish-.text: Social Democrat Leader Magdalena Andersson is on course to become Sweden’s next prime minister as her left-wing bloc holds an unassailable lead over the right and far right with 99.9% of results declared. By 10.30 p.m. on Wednesday night, Andersson’s four-party grouping was three seats ahead of Ulf Kristersson’s alliance of the right and far-right parties in the race to control the 349-seat parliament. The Swedish Election Authority is set to confirm the “preliminary” result when all the votes have finished being counted, expected on Thursday. Advertisement Advertisement The election is one of the closest in recent Swedish history, and offered voters a sharp choice between electing a new left-wing government or allowing far-right ministers into power for the first time. Swedish public broadcaster SVT called the election for Andersson’s side on Wednesday night. Her Social Democrats are Sweden’s biggest party and have enjoyed the loose support of three other opposition parties who are seen as her likely coalition partners: The Greens, the Center Party, and the Left Party. Kristersson’s conservative Moderates have been campaigning alongside the Christian Democrats, the Liberals and the far-right, anti-immigration Sweden Democrats. His allies do not expect him to concede defeat until Andersson wins a vote in parliament to prove she can command a majority. That vote won’t happen before Sept. 29 at the earliest. Coalition negotiations will begin in earnest once the final outcome is confirmed. In theory any combination of parties can form into a government but in reality, the two-bloc system is likely to hold, meaning Andersson will seek to govern with some or all of her left-leaning partner parties. Andersson’s Social Democrats stand on 99 seats, with her most natural allies in the Greens on 22. But that still leaves her 54 seats short of a majority and with a potentially difficult task persuading the other two parties in her bloc to cooperate with each other. The Left Party, which has a historic association with communists, is emboldened by increasing its seat tally at this election to 30. And it has said the price of supporting a government will be gaining ministers inside the new top team. Advertisement Advertisement But the Center Party’s leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist has said she cannot support this, because the “fringes” must not dominate the next government. Thand Ringqvist, whose party is set to take 25 seats — enough to get Andersson’s bloc a majority — ideally wants to form a new centrist administration without either the Left Party or the far-right Sweden Democrats. But the parliamentary numbers do not add up to a majority for such a grouping. The Center Party has said it will start talks with Andersson’s Social Democrats. Thand Ringqvist was clear on Wednesday night that Kristersson’s rightwing bloc had “lost their government mandate.” But she told SVT that “at the same time, the election result, as it stands, does not give a mandate for a political left turn.” Kristersson had promised to elevate representatives of the far-right Sweden Democrats into ministerial positions in his government if he won. In the end, while his Moderates party increased their vote share, the SD fell backwards, bucking the recent trend that had seen far right populists gain ground elsewhere in Europe. https://nineoclock.ro/jeongwoo-lee-18-ye.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Jeongwoo Lee, 18, Wins First Prize in the Piano Section of the 2026 George Enescu International Competition South Korean pianist Jeongwoo Lee, aged 18, has won First Prize in the Piano Section of the 2026 George Enescu International Competition, along with five special awards, following the Final held on Saturday, 19 September, at the Romanian Athenaeum. Jeongwoo Lee received the “Radu Lupu” Prize for the best performance of a work by George Enescu, the Prize for the Best Performance of the Commissioned Work, Hammers and Tongs by Karim Al-Zand, the Audience Prize, the “Playing for Tomorrow” Prize, offered by BRD – Groupe Société Générale, and the École Cortot Prize. Second Prize was awarded to Yiming Guo from China, while Third Prize went to Pin-Hong Lin from Taiwan. The three finalists performed on the stage of the Romanian Athenaeum alongside the George Enescu Philharmonic Orchestra , conducted by Daniela Candillari , in a concert that brought the Piano Section and the 20th edition of the George Enescu International Competition to a close. In the final, Jeongwoo Lee performed Frédéric Chopin’s Piano Concerto No. 2 in F minor, Op. 21; Yiming Guo performed Sergei Prokofiev’s Piano Concerto No. 3 in C major, Op. 26; and Pin-Hong Lin performed Johannes Brahms’s Piano Concerto No. 2 in B-flat major, Op. 83. The results of the Piano Section were determined by the international jury chaired by Lilya Zilberstein , whose members included Nelson Goerner, Rena Shereshevskaya, Marie-Ange Nguci, Vovka Ashkenazy, Didier de Cottignies, Dana Borșan, Anthony Fog g and Raluca Știrbăț . In addition to First Prize, Jeongwoo Lee received five special awards: the “Radu Lupu” Prize , worth €3,000, for the best performance of a work by George Enescu — Piano Suite No. 2 in D major, Op. 10; the Prize for the Best Performance of the Commissioned Work , Hammers and Tongs by Karim Al-Zand, worth €2,000; the Audience Prize , worth €1,000; and the “Playing for Tomorrow” Prize , worth €1,500, offered by BRD – Groupe Société Générale. Jeongwoo Lee also received the École Cortot Prize , which consists of an opportunity to perform a recital at the prestigious Salle Cortot in Paris during the 2028–2029 season, as part of the venue’s centenary celebrations. The prize was announced in Bucharest by Murielle Hurel, Director of the École Normale de Musique de Paris. The connection between Alfred Cortot and George Enescu holds particular significance: the two were close friends who performed together, and Enescu taught at the École Normale de Musique de Paris in the 1930s. The “Constanța Erbiceanu” Prize , awarded to the highest-ranked Romanian competitor in the Piano Section, went to pianist Inya-Maria Cutova . For each of the three instrumental sections of the George Enescu International Competition — Cello, Violin and Piano — First Prize is worth €15,000, Second Prize €10,000, and Third Prize €5,000. Beyond the monetary awards, the George Enescu International Competition offers laureates opportunities designed to support the development of their international careers. ARTEXIM awards prizes consisting of concerts and recitals at the 2027 and 2028 editions of the George Enescu International Festival and Competition, as well as performances during the 2026–2028 seasons of concert halls and performing arts institutions in Romania. These opportunities are developed in partnership with the Lyra – George Cavadia Philharmonic in Brăila, Arad Philharmonic, “Mihail Jora” Philharmonic in Bacău, “Oltenia” Philharmonic in Craiova, “Moldova” Philharmonic in Iași, Oradea State Philharmonic, Pitești Philharmonic, “Paul Constantinescu” Philharmonic in Ploiești, “Ion Dumitrescu” Philharmonic in Râmnicu Vâlcea, “Dinu Lipatti” State Philharmonic in Satu Mare, Sibiu State Philharmonic and the National Chamber Orchestra of Chișinău. As part of the 2026 edition, Andreas Vierziger , music curator and strategist, will offer the winners and laureates of the instrumental sections mentoring sessions and personalised consultancy tailored to their professional needs and goals. The programme addresses essential aspects of developing an international career, including artistic positioning, strategic career development, relationships with the music industry and identifying relevant professional opportunities. The George Enescu International Competition trophy was created by artist Mihai Băncilă. Jeongwoo Lee Jeongwoo Lee (South Korea), born on 23 January 2008 in Seongnam, is currently pursuing his undergraduate studies at the New England Conservatory under the guidance of Professor HaeSun Paik. In 2020, he won First Prize at the Ewha Kyunghyang Music Competition, one of South Korea’s most prestigious competitions for young musicians. He graduated from Yewon School with the distinction of “Outstanding Performance” and had the opportunity to perform a piano concerto with the school orchestra. In 2024, he won First Prize at the Ettlingen International Piano Competition and participated in the Morningside Music Bridge programme at the New England Conservatory in Boston, receiving a full scholarship. Yiming Guo Yiming Guo (China), born on 13 November 2001, is currently pursuing postgraduate studies at the Central Conservatory of Music in Beijing under the guidance of Professor Danwen Wei. He has won numerous prizes at piano competitions, including the 2022 Long-Thibaud Competition and the 2024 Xiamen International Piano Competition. In 2025, he received an additional award for “Best Chinese Pianist” at the Paderewski Piano Competition. He was also a semifinalist at the 2026 Takamatsu International Piano Competition. Pin-Hong Lin Pin-Hong Lin (Taiwan), born on 30 July 2001, is currently pursuing an Artist Diploma at the Jacobs School of Music under the guidance of Professor Norman Krieger. He also receives artistic guidance from Xin Wang, Artistic Director of the Euregio Piano Award. Recently, he won Third Prize and the award for Best Performance of a Classical Sonata at the Paderewski International Piano Competition, as well as the Hastings Prize at the Hastings International Piano Competition. Other distinctions include Second Prize at the Philadelphia International Piano Competition and Third Prize at the Maria Canals Piano Competition. As a soloist, he has performed concertos with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, the Pomeranian Philharmonic, the Barcelona Youth Symphony Orchestra, Sinfonia Smith Square, the Taipei Symphony Orchestra, the National Symphony Orchestra of Taiwan and the New Music Ensemble. The 2026 edition of the George Enescu International Competition took place in Bucharest from 23 August to 19 September , under the theme “In Pursuit of Excellence”, and received a record 819 applications from 58 countries — 756 for the competition and 63 for the masterclasses held as part of the event. https://www.dw.com/en/us-federal-agents-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OAsK The US Justice Department did not share details of their investigation Image: Annabelle Gordon/REUTERS Advertisement US federal agents searched the home of a Democratic congresswoman and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump on Monday, the Department of Justice (DoJ) confirmed. Officials from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of US immigration enforcement, were seen early on Monday morning outside the Washington home of Ilhan Omar . "Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice," a DoJ spokesperson told the Reuters news agency in a statement which didn't specifically name Omar. "This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation." Who is Ilhan Omar? Omar, who came to the United States from Somalia as a child, was first elected to Congress in 2018 and is a member of the group of left-wing Democratic lawmakers known as "The Squad," who have been among Trump's most vocal opponents. Omar represents a district including Minneapolis, home to one of the largest Somali communities in the US – a community which Trump has frequently targeted in racist outbursts . Omar has said Trump has a 'creepy obsession' with her Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance He ​previously called Somalis "garbage" and said in February that Omar and Democratic Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan should be "institutionalized" and sent back to "where they came from." Last ​week, Trump called Democratic candidate for US Senate from Michigan Abdul El Sayed a "RADICAL Extremist" and "Terrorist Sympathizer" while offering support for the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers Democrats decry 'abuse of power' House Democratic leaders condemned the search as an "abuse of power" by the Trump administration. Omar said she will “not be silenced” and called the search of her home the “latest escalation” in President Donald Trump’s '‘intimidation" campaign. Trump has been accused of weaponizing US agenices to go after his political opponents Image: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance Omar has called Trump's focus on her an "unhealthy and creepy obsession" said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes ⁠to "hateful political rhetoric" especially ​from Trump. On Monday, Omar said she will "not be silenced" and called the search of her home the "latest escalation" in Trump's "intimidation" campaign. No charges against Omar were announced in connection with Monday's search, but US media reported that the operation was linked to a criminal fraud investigation into immigration paperwork submitted on her behalf by her late father when she was a child. The search comes just three weeks before midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans will be trying to defend their thin majorities in the US. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: A US navy jet lands at Kadena air base in Okinawa, Japan. The US military has banned vehicles made by China’s BYD at the base. Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A US navy jet lands at Kadena air base in Okinawa, Japan. The US military has banned vehicles made by China’s BYD at the base. Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images Japan US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis Justin McCurry in Tokyo Mon 26 Oct 2026 22.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday. The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa , has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information. “These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement. ‘BYD effect’: electric vehicle boom becomes unexpected tool to combat inflation Read more The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around. Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China , Russia or North Korea . Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website. View image in fullscreen A US military plane takes off at Kadena air force base on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa. Photograph: Issei Kato/Reuters The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said. American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners. In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu. The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns. China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association. BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025. It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan , where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.
